title: Reading Lagoon
description: Read new short passages for detail, inference, reasons, vocabulary in context and main ideas.

questions.prompt:
THE UNLABELLED ALBUM
Nadia found an album while helping her aunt tidy a cupboard. Several photographs had no names or dates. At first, she wanted to label them by guessing. Her aunt suggested asking relatives instead. One uncle recognised a village square, but he was unsure about the year. Nadia wrote his suggestion in pencil and added a question mark. After two more interviews, she corrected one date. At the school display, she explained how her information had changed. Her teacher praised her careful checking, not the number of photographs. Nadia decided to keep a separate list of facts that still needed evidence.

Why did Nadia speak to relatives?
options: To invite them to a village festival.
To identify information missing from the photographs.
To ask them to buy an album.
questions.explanation: The photographs lacked names and dates, so relatives could help identify them.

questions.prompt:
A THOUGHTFUL PRESENT
Before a class visit to a community centre, pupils planned to buy a large glass ornament for the organiser. Karim noticed that the centre had little shelf space and that young children often used the room. He suggested asking what would be useful. The organiser mentioned that the reading corner needed new books. The pupils chose several books and wrote friendly messages on separate cards. Karim worried that books would seem less exciting than an ornament. During the visit, however, he saw children reading them straight away. He realised that a useful gift could show care better than an expensive decoration.

Why did Karim question the first gift idea?
options: It might be unsuitable for the room.
He wanted to keep the ornament.
questions.explanation: Limited shelf space and young children made a large glass ornament less suitable.

questions.prompt:
THE QUIET GUIDE
Leen volunteered to guide visitors around the school exhibition. She knew the displays well, but speaking to unfamiliar adults worried her. On the first day, she read every word from a long script. Some visitors stopped listening. Her partner suggested using three short notes and asking visitors what interested them. Leen tried this with the next group. A visitor asked about a family recipe display, so she spent longer there and skipped a section they had already seen. By the end of the afternoon, she was still a little nervous, but she could speak more naturally. She planned to practise again before the next event.

What worried Leen at first?
options: Speaking to adults she did not know.
questions.explanation: She knew the displays but felt worried about unfamiliar adults.

questions.prompt:
THE CHANGING ROUTE
For a local-history project, Rami drew a walking route past four old buildings. He checked the distances on a map but did not visit the streets first. During a practice walk, his group found that the bridge near the last building was closed. Rami wanted to remove the building from the project. His friend suggested a different path through the park. It took ten extra minutes, but it passed a useful information board about the town. They added that stop and changed the start time so the walk would still finish before lunch. Rami learned that planning on paper was only the beginning.

What had Rami failed to do before the practice walk?
options: Measure the distances on a map.
questions.explanation: He used a map but had not visited the streets first.

questions.prompt:
THE RECIPE NOTEBOOK
Sara wanted to collect recipes for a family booklet. Her grandfather described a soup but used phrases such as 'a little rice' and 'enough water'. Sara could not turn these into clear instructions. She asked to cook it with him and measured the ingredients as they worked. The first bowl tasted different from his usual soup because she had added the salt too early. Her grandfather explained when to add it. Sara changed her notes and included a small warning for readers. The finished booklet recorded both the ingredients and the order of the steps. Sara discovered that watching and trying could teach her things that an interview alone could not.

Why were the first instructions difficult to follow?
options: Sara could not read the language.
questions.explanation: Phrases such as a little and enough did not give exact measurements.

questions.prompt:
A SMALL EXHIBITION
The history club wanted to fill a hall with displays for the school anniversary. With only a week left, the pupils had collected many objects but had little reliable information about them. Their teacher asked visitors what they would want to learn. The answers showed that clear stories mattered more than the number of objects. The club chose five items with well-supported histories. They used large labels and added an audio recording for visitors who preferred listening. Some pupils worried that the hall would look empty. On the day, visitors spent time discussing the five objects rather than rushing past crowded tables. The club decided that a smaller display could still be successful.

What difficulty did the club face?
options: They had no objects at all.
Visitors refused to enter the school.
Many objects had little reliable information.
questions.explanation: The pupils had collected many items but knew little reliable information about them.
